0.title: Citizens of Heaven, Neighbours on Earth
0.overview:
How should Christians relate to the world around them? To government, politics, culture, their neighbours and their nation? Christians have answered in very different ways. Some withdraw, building separate communities and keeping their distance from public life. Others try to take over, seeing politics as the main way to advance God's kingdom. Many simply absorb the values of their culture without noticing.

Jesus prayed for his disciples, I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world (John 17:15-16). Christians are in the world but not of it. We are citizens of heaven, living for now as sojourners and exiles (1 Pet 2:11). Yet God calls us to seek the good of the places where we live, to honour those in authority, to do justice and love mercy, and to shine as lights.

This study asks how Christians can live faithfully in public life: neither withdrawing nor being swallowed up. Some of these questions are disputed among faithful Christians, and the study tries to distinguish clear biblical principles from matters of wisdom where believers may differ.

Six units: (1) Exiles and Citizens; (2) God and Government; (3) When We Must Obey God Rather than Men; (4) Christians and Politics; (5) Salt, Light and Worldliness; (6) Loving Our Neighbour and Seeking Justice.

1.title: Exiles and Citizens
1.overview:
Citizens of heaven. But our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ (Phil 3:20). A Christian's deepest loyalty is to Christ and his kingdom. Every earthly nation is temporary. This frees us from idolising any country, party or leader.

Exiles on earth. Peter writes to believers as elect exiles (1 Pet 1:1) and urges them as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh (1 Pet 2:11). Exiles live in a land that is not their final home. They are not fully at home in its culture or values. This explains why Christians often feel out of step with the world around them. We are meant to.

Seeking the good of the city. Yet exile is not withdrawal. When Judah was taken into exile in Babylon, God told them through Jeremiah, Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce... seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare (Jer 29:5, 7). God's people were to work, marry, raise families and pray for a pagan city. Christians today are called to the same: to be good neighbours, workers and citizens wherever God has placed them.

Good conduct as witness. Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation (1 Pet 2:12). Christians will be misunderstood and criticised. Our answer is not anger or withdrawal but consistent goodness, which over time speaks for itself.

Sent into the world. Jesus said, As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world (John 17:18). Christians are not in the world by accident. We are sent. Every workplace, neighbourhood and nation is a mission field.
1.theology:
Two kingdoms or one Lord? Christians have long distinguished between the spiritual realm, where Christ rules his church by his word and Spirit, and the civil realm, where God rules through governments and common grace. Both belong to God, but they work differently. The church does not wield the sword, and the state does not preach the gospel. Christ is Lord of both.

Common grace: God gives good gifts to all people, believers and unbelievers: rain, harvest, family, government, art, science and justice (Matt 5:45; Acts 14:17). Christians can appreciate and work alongside unbelievers for the common good, while knowing that only the gospel saves.

Patriotism and its limits: Loving one's country, praying for it and serving it are good. But patriotism becomes idolatry when national identity is placed above Christ, or when Christians of other nations are seen as less our brothers and sisters than unbelieving fellow citizens.
1.examples:
Then: Daniel and his friends were taken to Babylon as young men. They learned the language and literature of Babylon and served in its government. But they refused to defile themselves with the king's food or worship his gods (Dan 1:8; 3:18). They served the city faithfully without surrendering their loyalty to God.

Now: A Christian family moves to a city where few people go to church. They are tempted either to retreat into a Christian bubble or to blend in quietly. Instead, they get to know their neighbours, join a local community group, host street parties and pray for their area. Over the years, several neighbours come to church with them.

A simple test: Where has God placed you? What would it look like to seek the welfare of that place this month?

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus says the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, to all the exiles whom I have sent into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon: Build houses and live in them; plant gardens and eat their produce. Take wives and have sons and daughters; take wives for your sons, and give your daughters in marriage, that they may bear sons and daughters; multiply there, and do not decrease. But seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you into exile, and pray to the LORD on its behalf, for in its welfare you will find your welfare. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The exiles in Babylon wanted to go home, and false prophets told them they soon would. God told them to settle in, build, plant and marry. And astonishingly, to pray for Babylon, the enemy city. Their welfare was tied to its welfare. God's people are to be a blessing wherever they live, even among those who do not share their faith.

verseByVerse.quote: Beloved, I urge you as sojourners and exiles to abstain from the passions of the flesh, which wage war against your soul. Keep your conduct among the Gentiles honorable, so that when they speak against you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day of visitation. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter reminds believers that they are sojourners and exiles. This shapes their conduct in two ways. Inwardly, they must fight sinful desires. Outwardly, they must live honourably among unbelievers, so that even those who slander them may come to glorify God. Holiness and good works are a powerful witness.

verseByVerse.quote: I have given them your word, and the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. Sanctify them in the truth; your word is truth. As you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus prays that his disciples will be kept from the evil one, not removed from the world. They are not of the world, just as he is not. They are sanctified by the truth of God's word. And they are sent into the world, as he was. Christian life is lived in tension: different from the world, sent to the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Brothers, join in imitating me, and keep your eyes on those who walk according to the example you have in us. For many, of whom I have often told you and now tell you even with tears, walk as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things. But our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body, by the power that enables him even to subject all things to himself. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul contrasts two kinds of people: those whose minds are set on earthly things, and those whose citizenship is in heaven. Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens were proud of their Roman citizenship. Paul says believers have a higher citizenship. They await a Saviour who will transform their bodies and subject all things to himself.

1.reflection:
In what ways do you feel like an "exile" in your culture? Is that a good or bad thing?

Read Jeremiah 29:4-7. What would it mean to seek the welfare of your town or city?

How can good conduct silence those who speak against Christians?

What is the difference between healthy patriotism and idolatry of one's nation?

2.title: God and Government
2.overview:
Government is God's servant. Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God (Rom 13:1). Paul wrote this under Nero, the emperor who would later persecute Christians in Rome. Government is not a human invention or a necessary evil. It is God's institution, given to restrain evil and promote good.

What government is for. Paul explains that rulers are God's servant for your good, and that the ruler does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer (Rom 13:4). Government's main task is justice: protecting the innocent, punishing wrongdoers and maintaining order so that people can live peaceful lives. Peter says governors are sent to punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good (1 Pet 2:14).

What Christians owe. Christians owe government submission, taxes, respect and honour (Rom 13:7). Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the emperor (1 Pet 2:17). This includes obeying laws, paying taxes honestly and speaking of leaders with respect, even when we disagree with them.

Pray for those in authority. First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way (1 Tim 2:1-2). Paul tells Timothy to make this the first priority in the church's prayers. Christians should pray regularly for their national and local leaders, including those they did not vote for.

God rules over rulers. He removes kings and sets up kings (Dan 2:21). No ruler holds power except by God's permission, and every ruler will answer to him. This gives Christians peace when governments are bad, and humility when governments are good.
2.theology:
Government is limited: Government is God's servant, not God. It has authority in its sphere, but not over conscience or the church's worship and teaching. When government claims divine authority, as Rome did when it demanded emperor worship, it oversteps its role.

Justice, not salvation: Government cannot save, transform hearts or bring in God's kingdom. Its role is limited to justice and order. Christians who expect government to accomplish what only the gospel can do will be disappointed.

Paying taxes: Jesus said, Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's (Matt 22:21). Taxes belong to the government; our whole selves belong to God. Christians should pay taxes honestly, even when they disagree with how the money is spent.
2.examples:
Then: Joseph served as second-in-command in Egypt, a pagan empire. Through his wise administration, he saved Egypt and many nations from famine (Gen 41). Daniel served several kings with integrity. God's people have often served faithfully in governments that did not share their faith.

Now: A Christian strongly dislikes his country's leader and often speaks of him with contempt on social media. Reading 1 Timothy 2:1-2 and 1 Peter 2:17, he is convicted. He still disagrees with the leader's policies and says so respectfully, but he begins to pray for him by name each week and to stop mocking him online.

A simple test: When did you last pray by name for your national and local leaders?

verseByVerse.quote: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities. For there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been instituted by God. Therefore whoever resists the authorities resists what God has appointed, and those who resist will incur judgment. For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad. Would you have no fear of the one who is in authority? Then do what is good, and you will receive his approval, for he is God's servant for your good. But if you do wrong, be afraid, for he does not bear the sword in vain. For he is the servant of God, an avenger who carries out God's wrath on the wrongdoer. Therefore one must be in subjection, not only to avoid God's wrath but also for the sake of conscience. For because of this you also pay taxes, for the authorities are ministers of God, attending to this very thing. Pay to all what is owed to them: taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed, respect to whom respect is owed, honor to whom honor is owed. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul grounds the authority of government in God's appointment. Rulers are God's servants for good, bearing the sword to punish evil. Christians should submit not only to avoid punishment but for the sake of conscience. Taxes, revenue, respect and honour are owed. Government is not perfect, but it is God's gift for restraining evil.

verseByVerse.quote: Be subject for the Lord's sake to every human institution, whether it be to the emperor as supreme, or to governors as sent by him to punish those who do evil and to praise those who do good. For this is the will of God, that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people. Live as people who are free, not using your freedom as a cover-up for evil, but living as servants of God. Honor everyone. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honor the emperor. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter writes to Christians facing hostility. He tells them to submit to human institutions for the Lord's sake. Their good conduct will silence foolish critics. They are free, but must not use freedom as a cover for evil. And he sums up their duties in four short commands: honour everyone, love the brotherhood, fear God, honour the emperor.

verseByVerse.quote: First of all, then, I urge that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high positions, that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified in every way. This is good, and it is pleasing in the sight of God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The church's first prayer priority includes kings and those in authority. The goal is a peaceful and quiet life, godly and dignified. Peace and order make it easier for the gospel to spread. And God desires all people to be saved, including rulers.

verseByVerse.quote: Daniel answered and said: "Blessed be the name of God forever and ever, to whom belong wisdom and might. He changes times and seasons; he removes kings and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who have understanding; he reveals deep and hidden things; he knows what is in the darkness, and the light dwells with him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Daniel praises God after receiving the meaning of the king's dream. God changes times and seasons, removes kings and sets up kings. He gives wisdom and reveals deep things. The most powerful ruler on earth was under God's sovereign hand. So is every ruler today.

2.reflection:
Why is it significant that Paul wrote Romans 13 under a pagan emperor?

What does government exist to do, according to Romans 13 and 1 Peter 2?

How can you honour leaders you disagree with?

Make a list of national and local leaders to pray for this week.

3.title: When We Must Obey God Rather than Men
3.overview:
Submission to government is the normal Christian duty. But it is not absolute. When human authorities command what God forbids, or forbid what God commands, Christians must obey God.

The apostles' example. When the Jewish council ordered Peter and John not to speak or teach in Jesus' name, they answered, Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge, for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard (Acts 4:19-20). Later, arrested again, they said, We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29). They did not riot or rebel. They respectfully refused, continued preaching and accepted the consequences, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name (Acts 5:41).

Old Testament examples. The Hebrew midwives refused Pharaoh's order to kill baby boys, and God blessed them (Exod 1:17, 20). Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego refused to bow to Nebuchadnezzar's image: But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up (Dan 3:18). Daniel continued to pray despite the king's decree (Dan 6:10).

The pattern. These examples share common features. The command required clear disobedience to God. The believers refused openly, not deceitfully where possible. They were respectful, not contemptuous. They accepted the penalty. And they trusted God with the outcome.

Persecution. Jesus warned his followers that they would be hated for his name (John 15:18-20). Across the world today, many Christians face imprisonment, violence and death. Believers in freer countries should pray for them, support them and prepare their own hearts. Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted (2 Tim 3:12).
3.theology:
Resistance: the views. Some Christians hold that believers may only refuse to obey sinful commands, never actively resist government. Others, in a long strand of Reformed thought, have argued that when rulers become tyrants, lower officials (such as regional governors or parliaments) may lawfully resist them to protect the people. Some have gone further, justifying revolution by private citizens.

The verdict: The New Testament pattern for individual Christians is refusal to sin, respectful speech and patient endurance, not violent rebellion. Christians may use lawful means to resist injustice: courts, elections, petitions, peaceful protest. Lawful authorities may have a duty to restrain a ruler who destroys justice. But private believers are never called to take up the sword against government on their own authority (Rom 12:19).

Not every disagreement: Disliking a policy, paying high taxes or losing an election does not justify disobedience. The line is drawn when obedience would require sin.
3.examples:
Then: The midwives Shiphrah and Puah feared God more than Pharaoh. They let the boys live. When challenged, they did not defy Pharaoh openly but protected the babies. So God dealt well with the midwives (Exod 1:20). Their names are remembered; the Pharaoh's is not.

Now: A Christian nurse is asked to take part directly in a procedure that ends a human life. She respectfully explains her conscientious objection to her manager, offers to care for other patients and accepts that she may face consequences at work. She is not aggressive or self-righteous, but she will not do what God forbids.

A simple test: Is there anything in your work or public life that would require you to disobey God? How would you respond respectfully and firmly?

verseByVerse.quote: So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. But Peter and John answered them, "Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge, for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter and John had healed a lame man and preached Christ. The council ordered them to stop. Their answer is a model of respectful firmness. They invited the council to judge for itself, but they could not stop speaking of what they had seen and heard. Witness to Christ is not optional.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had brought them, they set them before the council. And the high priest questioned them, saying, "We strictly charged you not to teach in this name, yet here you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and you intend to bring this man's blood upon us." But Peter and the apostles answered, "We must obey God rather than men. The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree. God exalted him at his right hand as Leader and Savior, to give repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins. And we are witnesses to these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Arrested again, the apostles were reminded of the council's order. Peter answered simply: we must obey God rather than men. He then preached the gospel to the council itself. The apostles were beaten, and they left rejoicing. Obedience to God cost them, but it did not crush their joy.

verseByVerse.quote: Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego answered and said to the king, "O Nebuchadnezzar, we have no need to answer you in this matter. If this be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of your hand, O king. But if not, be it known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden image that you have set up." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The three young men faced a furnace. They did not need to defend themselves. Their God was able to deliver them. And even if he did not, they would not bow. Their faith did not depend on a guaranteed rescue. It depended on God's worth.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was named Shiphrah and the other Puah, "When you serve as midwife to the Hebrew women and see them on the birthstool, if it is a son, you shall kill him, but if it is a daughter, she shall live." But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but let the male children live. So the king of Egypt called the midwives and said to them, "Why have you done this, and let the male children live?" The midwives said to Pharaoh, "Because the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife comes to them." So God dealt well with the midwives. And the people multiplied and grew very strong. And because the midwives feared God, he gave them families. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Pharaoh ordered the Hebrew midwives to kill newborn boys. They feared God and did not obey. God blessed them and gave them families. The fear of God gave them courage to defy the most powerful man in the world to protect the vulnerable.

3.reflection:
What are the marks of faithful Christian disobedience in Acts 4-5 and Daniel 3?

Where is the line between submission to government and obedience to God?

How can Christians in free countries support persecuted believers elsewhere?

Read Daniel 3:16-18. How does "but if not" shape your faith?

4.title: Christians and Politics
4.overview:
Politics stirs strong feelings, and Christians are often divided by it. Scripture does not give a party platform, but it gives principles that should shape every believer's engagement.

Justice matters to God. Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people (Prov 14:34). God cares how nations are governed. The prophets condemned rulers who oppressed the poor, took bribes and shed innocent blood. Do justice and righteousness, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. And do no wrong or violence to the resident alien, the fatherless, and the widow, nor shed innocent blood (Jer 22:3). Christians should care about laws that protect life, family, justice and the vulnerable.

Some issues are clear. Scripture speaks plainly on some matters: the sanctity of human life from conception to natural death, the definition of marriage, honesty, the protection of the poor and the vulnerable, and religious freedom. Christians should be clear on these.

Many issues are matters of wisdom. Many political questions, such as tax rates, economic policy, healthcare systems or immigration levels, involve how best to apply shared principles. Faithful Christians can disagree about them. Churches should not bind consciences on matters where Scripture does not speak clearly.

Engagement without idolatry. Christians may vote, campaign, serve in office and speak publicly. But no party or candidate is the Messiah. When political identity becomes stronger than Christian identity, idolatry has crept in. Our hope is not in elections but in Christ, whose kingdom will never end.

Speech and civility. Christians must speak truthfully and graciously about political opponents. Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt (Col 4:6). Slander, mockery and outrage are no less sinful in politics than anywhere else.
4.theology:
The church and politics: the views. Some argue the church should actively campaign for political change and endorse candidates. Others argue the church should be silent on public issues and focus only on personal salvation. Some hold that civil law should be based directly on the Old Testament law of Israel (theonomy).

The verdict: The church's mission is to preach the gospel, make disciples and teach all that Christ commanded, including his moral law, which has public implications. Pulpits should proclaim clear biblical truth, but not endorse parties or candidates. Individual Christians, shaped by the church's teaching, engage in public life as salt and light. The civil laws of Israel expired with Israel as a nation, though their underlying justice still instructs us.

Unity in the church: Christians of different political views must worship together as one body. The church is not a political party at prayer.
4.examples:
Then: John the Baptist rebuked King Herod for taking his brother's wife (Mark 6:18). He was not campaigning for office. He was faithfully speaking God's word to a ruler, and it cost him his life. Prophetic courage is sometimes required.

Now: Two church members support different political parties and have argued bitterly online. Their pastor brings them together. They agree on the clear biblical issues, acknowledge that they differ on matters of wisdom and commit to speak of each other and of opponents with respect. They remain friends, and they pray together for their nation.

A simple test: Does your political identity shape your faith more than your faith shapes your politics?

verseByVerse.quote: Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Nations are not neutral before God. Righteousness lifts them up; sin brings disgrace. God judges nations as well as individuals, as the prophets made clear. Christians who care about their nation will care about its righteousness, not only its prosperity or power.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Go down to the house of the king of Judah and speak there this word, and say, 'Hear the word of the LORD, O king of Judah, who sits on the throne of David, you, and your servants, and your people who enter these gates. Thus says the LORD: Do justice and righteousness, and deliver from the hand of the oppressor him who has been robbed. And do no wrong or violence to the resident alien, the fatherless, and the widow, nor shed innocent blood in this place. For if you will indeed obey this word, then there shall enter the gates of this house kings who sit on the throne of David, riding in chariots and on horses, they and their servants and their people. But if you will not obey these words, I swear by myself, declares the LORD, that this house shall become a desolation. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God sends Jeremiah to the king's palace with a message: do justice, deliver the oppressed, protect the vulnerable, shed no innocent blood. If the king obeys, his dynasty will continue. If not, the palace will become a ruin. God holds rulers accountable for how they use their power.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to entangle him in his words. And they sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying, "Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully, and you do not care about anyone's opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances. Tell us, then, what you think. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?" But Jesus, aware of their malice, said, "Why put me to the test, you hypocrites? Show me the coin for the tax." And they brought him a denarius. And Jesus said to them, "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" They said, "Caesar's." Then he said to them, "Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's." When they heard it, they marveled. And they left him and went away. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The Pharisees tried to trap Jesus with a question about taxes. If he said pay, he would anger the people; if he said don't, he would be accused of rebellion. Jesus asked whose image was on the coin. Caesar's. So give Caesar what is his. And give God what is his. The coin bears Caesar's image; we bear God's.

verseByVerse.quote: "With what shall I come before the LORD, and bow myself before God on high? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old? Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, with ten thousands of rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?" He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Micah asks what God really wants. Not endless sacrifices, but this: to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God. These three belong together. Justice without kindness becomes harsh; kindness without justice becomes weak; both without humility before God become pride.

4.reflection:
Which political issues does Scripture speak to clearly? Which are matters of wisdom?

How can Christians engage in politics without making it an idol?

What does "render to Caesar" mean for you today?

How can you speak about political opponents in a way that honours Christ?

5.title: Salt, Light and Worldliness
5.overview:
Salt and light. Jesus told his disciples, You are the salt of the earth... You are the light of the world (Matt 5:13-14). Salt preserves and flavours. Light exposes and guides. Christians are to be a preserving, flavouring and illuminating presence in society. In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven (Matt 5:16).

The danger of losing saltiness. Jesus warned that salt that loses its taste is good for nothing (Matt 5:13). Christians who become indistinguishable from the world lose their influence. The church's power lies in its difference.

What is worldliness? Do not love the world or the things in the world... For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life—is not from the Father but is from the world (1 John 2:15-16). Worldliness is not enjoying creation, culture or good things. It is loving what the world loves in the way the world loves it: pleasure without God, possessions as identity, and status as the goal of life. A Christian can be worldly in a monastery and godly in a marketplace.

Do not be conformed. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind (Rom 12:2). The world presses us into its mould through media, advertising, education and peer pressure. The renewal of the mind comes through Scripture, prayer and Christian fellowship.

Engaging culture wisely. Christians can enjoy and create good art, music, literature and film, and can learn from unbelievers' work, because all truth and beauty come from God. But we must also discern. Paul quoted pagan poets in Athens (Acts 17:28) while being distressed by the city's idols (Acts 17:16). We need both appreciation and discernment.

Answer with gentleness. Always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect (1 Pet 3:15). Christians should be ready to explain their faith in public conversation, without arrogance or anger.
5.theology:
The world in Scripture: "The world" can mean the created order (which God made good), humanity (which God loves, John 3:16) or the system of human life organised in rebellion against God (which we must not love, 1 John 2:15). Distinguishing these meanings helps avoid both worldliness and unhealthy withdrawal.

Christ and culture: Christians have taken different approaches to culture: withdrawal from it, accommodation to it, or seeking to transform it. The New Testament calls for faithful presence: living distinctively within culture, contributing to its good, resisting its sin and pointing to Christ.

Liberty and love: In matters Scripture does not forbid, such as entertainment, food or drink in moderation, Christians have freedom. But that freedom is limited by love for weaker believers and by the danger of being mastered by anything (1 Cor 6:12; 8:9).
5.examples:
Then: In the early centuries, when plagues struck Roman cities, many fled. Christians were often noted for staying to care for the sick, including pagans. Their conduct drew attention to their faith. They were salt and light.

Now: A Christian student at university is mocked for her faith in a philosophy class. Instead of becoming defensive, she listens carefully, asks thoughtful questions and, when asked, gently explains why she believes. Several classmates later ask to talk more. Her gentleness was as persuasive as her arguments.

A simple test: In what area of your life are you most conformed to the world? What would it look like to be transformed?

verseByVerse.quote: "You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people's feet. "You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden. Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus does not say "try to be" salt and light. He says you are. Christians are already a distinctive presence in the world. The question is whether that presence is visible. A lamp hidden under a basket is useless. Good works, done openly and humbly, point people to the Father.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life—is not from the Father but is from the world. And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: John warns against loving the world. He names three ways it captures hearts: the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life. These are passing away. But whoever does the will of God abides forever. Worldliness is investing in what will not last.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you therefore, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and acceptable to God, which is your spiritual worship. Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: After eleven chapters of gospel, Paul calls believers to offer their whole lives to God. Then he warns against being squeezed into the world's mould. The alternative is transformation by the renewing of the mind. The result is the ability to discern God's good, acceptable and perfect will.

verseByVerse.quote: Now who is there to harm you if you are zealous for what is good? But even if you should suffer for righteousness' sake, you will be blessed. Have no fear of them, nor be troubled, but in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you; yet do it with gentleness and respect, having a good conscience, so that, when you are slandered, those who revile your good behavior in Christ may be put to shame. For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God's will, than for doing evil. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Peter writes to Christians facing suffering. They should not fear their opponents but honour Christ as Lord in their hearts. They should be ready to explain their hope, with gentleness and respect, and with a good conscience, so that those who slander them will be put to shame.

5.reflection:
What does it mean to be salt and light in your workplace or neighbourhood?

How would you define worldliness? Where do you see it in yourself?

How can Christians enjoy culture without being shaped by its sinful values?

Are you ready to explain the hope that is in you? Practise explaining it in two minutes.

6.title: Loving Our Neighbour and Seeking Justice
6.overview:
Who is my neighbour? A lawyer asked Jesus this question, hoping to limit his obligations. Jesus told the parable of the Good Samaritan, in which a despised foreigner cared for a wounded stranger while religious leaders passed by (Luke 10:29-37). Then he turned the question around: who proved to be a neighbor? The answer: The one who showed him mercy. And Jesus said, You go, and do likewise. Our neighbour is anyone in need whom God places in our path.

Doing good to all. So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith (Gal 6:10). Christians care first for fellow believers, but not only for them. We are called to do good to all.

Care for the vulnerable. Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world (Jas 1:27). God has a special concern for the poor, the fatherless, the widow and the foreigner (Deut 10:18). Throughout Scripture, God's people are called to reflect that concern.

Speak up for the voiceless. Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute. Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy (Prov 31:8-9). Christians should speak for those who cannot speak for themselves: the unborn, the trafficked, the abused, the persecuted and the poor.

Mercy and the gospel. Good works do not replace the gospel. People's greatest need is to be reconciled to God. But mercy adorns the gospel and opens doors for it. Jesus healed and preached; the early church fed widows and proclaimed Christ. Word and deed belong together.

Our final hope. No human effort will bring perfect justice. For here we have no lasting city, but we seek the city that is to come (Heb 13:14). Christians work for justice now, knowing it will be imperfect, while waiting for the King who will judge the world in righteousness and make all things new.
6.theology:
Justice in Scripture: Biblical justice means giving each person what is due under God's law: protecting rights, punishing wrongdoing fairly, showing no partiality and caring for the vulnerable. It is defined by God's character, not by any political ideology.

The church and mercy: The local church has a special responsibility to care for its own needy members (Acts 6; 1 Tim 5). Individual Christians and Christian organisations can also serve the wider community.

Loving our enemies: Jesus calls us to love even our enemies (Matt 5:44). This includes those who oppose us politically or persecute us for our faith. Christian love is not limited to those who love us back.
6.examples:
Then: Boaz, a wealthy landowner, allowed Ruth, a poor foreign widow, to glean in his fields and told his workers to leave extra grain for her (Ruth 2:15-16). He obeyed God's law for the poor, and went beyond it with kindness. His generosity became part of the story that led to David and to Christ.

Now: A church notices that many refugees have settled in their area. Members begin offering English classes, helping families navigate local services and inviting them into their homes. Some refugees become Christians. Others do not, but all have experienced Christ's love through his people.

A simple test: Who is the "wounded traveller" on your road? What would it mean to be a neighbour to them?

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a lawyer stood up to put him to the test, saying, "Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?" He said to him, "What is written in the Law? How do you read it?" And he answered, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself." And he said to him, "You have answered correctly; do this, and you will live." But he, desiring to justify himself, said to Jesus, "And who is my neighbor?" Jesus replied, "A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and he fell among robbers, who stripped him and beat him and departed, leaving him half dead. Now by chance a priest was going down that road, and when he saw him he passed by on the other side. So likewise a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side. But a Samaritan, as he journeyed, came to where he was, and when he saw him, he had compassion. He went to him and bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he set him on his own animal and brought him to an inn and took care of him. And the next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper, saying, 'Take care of him, and whatever more you spend, I will repay you when I come back.' Which of these three, do you think, proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell among the robbers?" He said, "The one who showed him mercy." And Jesus said to him, "You go, and do likewise." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The lawyer wanted to define his neighbour narrowly. Jesus told a story in which the hero was a Samaritan, a member of a despised group. The priest and Levite passed by. The Samaritan stopped, bandaged, carried and paid. Jesus' question changes everything: not "who is my neighbour?" but "am I being a neighbour?"

verseByVerse.quote: And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up. So then, as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who are of the household of faith. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul encourages believers not to grow weary of doing good, because in due season they will reap. As they have opportunity, they should do good to everyone, especially to fellow believers. Doing good is not a single act but a lifelong habit, and it is never wasted.

verseByVerse.quote: If anyone thinks he is religious and does not bridle his tongue but deceives his heart, this person's religion is worthless. Religion that is pure and undefiled before God the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their affliction, and to keep oneself unstained from the world. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: James defines pure religion in two ways: caring for orphans and widows in their distress, and keeping oneself unstained by the world. True religion is both compassionate and holy. Neither can be neglected.

verseByVerse.quote: Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute. Open your mouth, judge righteously, defend the rights of the poor and needy. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: These words come from a mother's advice to her son, a king. He is to use his position to speak up for those who cannot speak for themselves, to judge fairly and to defend the poor and needy. Power and influence are given to serve the vulnerable.

6.reflection:
Read Luke 10:25-37. Who are the people you tend to "pass by on the other side"?

How can you do good to those outside the church this month?

Who are the "voiceless" in your community that Christians should speak up for?

How do word and deed work together in Christian witness?
